Cyber Homebase

One front door for an enterprise security organization, so employees can find a policy, request a service, or report an incident without knowing who to ask.

Problem

Security resources were spread across old team sites, intake forms, and people's inboxes. Employees who needed a risk review or a policy answer often didn't know a formal process existed, so they went through whoever they knew. Security staff ended up pulled into the same requests repeatedly, and process knowledge lived in people's heads instead of anywhere findable.

That cost the company in three ways. Security staff got pulled into work that wasn't theirs. Compliance requirements were hard for other teams to follow. And the services the security team offered went unused, which left the company more exposed than it needed to be.

Process

DiscoverInterviewed security leads and subject-matter experts across each pillar. Mapped ownership and collected every existing policy, standard, process, and intake form.
DefineReviewed existing sites and service-ownership models. Set four principles: task-first navigation, only relevant content, modular structure, one front door.
DevelopBuild, learn the platform's limits, polish to brand standards, align with SMEs. Repeat.
DeliverLive homepage with migrated content, so scattered pages could be retired.

Key decisions

Navigate by task, not by org chart

People arrive with a job to do. The homepage leads with services ("I need a risk review", "I need access") and pushes team structure to its own page, where it answers who owns what.

Incident reporting sits above everything

The one action that can't wait got a persistent banner at the top of every visit instead of living in a menu.

Policies follow the governance hierarchy

Documents are grouped from top-level policy down to standards and procedures, so readers can see how a rule connects to the one above it.

Migrate everything, then retire the old pages

A new portal next to the old ones would add a fourth place to look. Moving all existing content and FAQs over made it possible to shut the scattered pages down. Processes with no home got one.

The hard one: security team vs. everyone else

The site had two audiences who wanted different things. The security team wanted a working hub for their own processes. Every other employee needed to find one thing fast and leave. One homepage couldn't put both first, so I compromised: the front page is built for general employees, and the security team's material lives in its own team-only section. The cost was that the people I worked with every day got a homepage that wasn't designed around them.

Side project: Cyber Pathways

A career-development map for the security team, aligning certifications to each pillar and to leadership's growth expectations. Mockup:

Outcome

Live company-wide with the reporting banner, service sections, policy center, and team pages. On handoff, the roadmap covered forms for the remaining pillars, a secured team-only area, and ownership moving to the governance team.

4 → 1Separate pages consolidated into one site
Company-wideCyber news, now pulled live into McLane's main employee site

SayStroop

The Stroop test has mostly lived in labs with a proctor and flashcards. We put it on the web: participants say their answers out loud and the app times them from the audio.

How it works

  • Sign in once. A name plus a generated ID blocks anyone from retaking the test.
  • Trial 1: say the ink color of each word. Trial 2, the control: read the word.
  • Audio is split per word, reaction time is measured, and both trials are written to Postgres.

Engineering problems

Whisper timestamps drift

Whisper is built for transcription, and its word timestamps were off enough to ruin a reaction-time measure. The fix: stop asking when a word was recognized and detect when sound started. A NumPy voice-activity detector, adapted from Silero VAD, marks the first energy spike above a noise threshold in each trial's audio. I built this with a teammate.

Streamlit reruns the whole script

Every interaction re-executes the app, which wipes anything not in session state. Each trial got its own session state and stored its data separately, then merged at the end for the database write.

Relational schema for one-shot participants

Two tables, stroop_users and stroop_trials, joined by UUID. Every trial row traces back to one person, and the user table doubles as the retake check.

Bridge

Only 7 of every 100 people who say they'll donate a kidney make it to surgery. Willingness isn't the problem. The process is isolating, clinical, and inconsistent.

What we found

Clinical evidence showed trained facilitators raise living donation rates. Interviews said the same thing in plainer terms: donors who heard consistent answers from mentors who'd been through it felt secure enough to keep going. The barriers were fear of complications despite low risk, family pressure and obligation, inconsistent guidance, and feeling alone.

Narrowing the audience

We started with both donors and recipients, then cut to donors only: specifically the 93 of 100 who drop off. Personas made it concrete. A willing donor scared of surgery and pressured by family needs a different moment of support than a resource portal can give.

Concept

Bridge matches each donor with a trained advocate who has lived the same journey, from first curiosity through workup, pre-op, recovery, and life after donation. One consistent human voice the whole way.

Where it went next

Bridge didn't stop at the design-a-thon. The work continues as BEACON, a UCSD Design Lab project with the REIMAGINE Center. In the second year of the Junior Designer program you're assigned to a real project, and this is mine. As a UX research consultant I work with both the research team and the technical team, carrying the donor research forward while the concept gets built.

Fire Scan

Homeowners in fire country live with constant low-grade dread because they can't tell how much time, money, or effort it would take to make their house safe.

Research

Six homeowner interviews, synthesized on sticky notes. People didn't lack motivation. They lacked clarity about what to fix and connections to people who could fix it. We explored fire prediction, evacuation planning, and satellite scanning, then focused on homeowner protection because it was underserved and the biggest source of anxiety.

Concept

A mobile app that scans the property with the phone camera and satellite imagery. A computer vision model, run on San Diego Supercomputer Center resources, flags risks in materials, vegetation, and objects near the house, rates each one, and recommends fixes with local contacts. Reports are shared with local government too.

DIB Passport

UCSD's Design and Innovation Building presents itself as open and collaborative. Most students we talked to found it intimidating and had no idea what each floor was for.

Research

We started with the building's websites, floor pages, social accounts, and Reddit threads, plus earlier Junior Designer research and comparable spaces on campus. Then we interviewed people at every distance from the building: staff, frequent visitors, infrequent visitors, and first-timers, with questions tailored to each. A survey of 60 students gave us patterns across a wider group.

Synthesis

I led this phase. I sorted findings from all three streams into physical space, accessibility, and culture and community, split each into what worked and what didn't, and ranked issues by how often they came up. The root cause was clear: no central, up-to-date source of information, so the building felt closed even though it isn't.

How might we

Help students feel welcome in the DIB and connected to the building as a whole, not just the one floor they happen to find?

Concept: the Passport Adventure

An interactive open house guided by a passport booklet. Visitors move floor by floor, collect two stamps per floor by doing short activities, and redeem a full passport for stickers. Each floor gets a resource page so the event leaves people knowing what to come back for. The idea borrows from what already works on campus: First Fridays, Welcome Week, and open houses.

Testing and refinement

We ran a scaled-down version with stations for the 3rd and 4th floors and measured it with pre-surveys, post-surveys, and dot voting. People got lost when activities shared a space, and random passersby needed the purpose explained up front. Changes that came out of it:

  • Every activity got its own space.
  • The passport went vertical, which made switching between notes and drawing easier.
  • Resource pages and note space were added for each floor, so contacts and programs stick.
  • A mascot gave the event a face for flyers and promotion, a pattern UCSD student orgs already use.

Making it real: logistics and feasibility

A concept that can't be staffed or scheduled never runs, and an event that confuses people at check-in recreates the exact problem it's solving. I owned whether this could actually happen, and wrote the plan that keeps it running: setup, check-in, stamp redemption, cleanup, staffing, capacity and accessibility, what to do when attendance runs over or under, and how often the event should repeat.

Delivered

Two physical passports, the digital passport pages, and the logistics plan, presented as the year-one final pitch.

About

I'm a Data Science student at UC San Diego with a Cognitive Science focus, and I work on both ends of a product. I find out what people actually need, then I build the thing.

At McLane I joined a cybersecurity team whose resources were scattered across old sites and inboxes. I interviewed the people answering the same requests over and over, then designed and engineered Cyber Homebase, the portal that replaced that sprawl. On SayStroop I built the backend that took a lab experiment onto anyone's laptop. On Bridge I led the research, and I've stayed with it as BEACON, working between the research and technical teams at the UCSD Design Lab.

Cognitive science is why I care how people perceive and decide. Data science is how I act on it. I want to build tools that make people more capable: better interfaces, applied AI, and technology that extends what people can perceive.
